tagline: Island roads, sandy beaches and old forts along New Hampshire’s coast
intro: The Coastal Byway follows NH 1A and 1B between Portsmouth and Seabrook, overlooking sandy beaches, rocky Gulf of Maine shores and the Hampton Seabrook Marsh. New Hampshire’s tourism division highlights the byway’s ocean views, historic forts and ten state-park units. The island section on 1B is narrow and winding; 1A follows the mainland shore as Ocean Boulevard. Visit NH gives a driving time of about an hour without stops. Along Hampton Beach, 1A is a divided four-lane highway directly beside the beaches; north of Winnacunnet Road, it narrows to two undivided lanes.

Bridges changed how travelers reached this coast. In 1821, three bridges opened a new connection from Portsmouth to New Castle’s Great Island; previously, the southwestern bridge was its only land approach. Farther south, Wallace D. Lovell’s wooden Hampton Bridge opened in 1901. Automobiles succeeded trolley cars, and the aging wooden crossing gave way to a replacement opened in 1949.

Travel south from Portsmouth on 1B across the causeway to New Castle, passing Fort Constitution and Fort Stark. Join 1A for Odiorne Point, then follow the shore through Rye and North Hampton to Hampton Beach. Beyond the beach, Hampton Bridge carries the road across the harbor inlet to Seabrook.
notice: The shore changes between sandy beaches and rock, with the Hampton Seabrook Marsh beside the byway.

moments.title: Fort Constitution
moments.text: The fort raided in December 1774 was called Fort William and Mary. On December 14, John Langdon led Portsmouth-area Patriots against its six-man caretaker detachment and seized the gunpowder supply. Rebels led by John Sullivan returned the next day for cannon, ammunition and supplies. The name Fort Constitution followed rebuilding completed in 1808. Workers doubled the height of the brick walls and added brick buildings inside, changing the colonial fort before its service in the War of 1812. The site also holds Portsmouth Harbor Light, completed in 1878, continuing a lighthouse presence that began here in 1771.

moments.title: Odiorne Point State Park
moments.text: Circular concrete gun platforms remain at Odiorne Point, part of the former Fort Dearborn. In 1942, the United States government condemned and bought private oceanfront property here to build coastal defenses. The guns themselves were scrapped in 1948, leaving the concrete structures as evidence of the military use of this shore. When the land passed to New Hampshire in 1961, former owners were not offered the chance to buy it back. The transfer required public recreation, and the park opened in July 1972. The Seacoast Science Center now has aquariums, touch tanks and whale skeletons within the park.
moments.notice: Circular concrete platforms survive from Fort Dearborn’s first gun battery.

moments.title: Hampton Beach
moments.text: Hampton Beach occupies a barrier spit, with Hampton Harbor’s estuary separating most of the resort village from the mainland. Ocean Boulevard runs along the beach beside the boardwalk. In the southern resort area, traffic divides between northbound Ocean Boulevard and southbound Ashworth Avenue, linked by cross streets lettered A through M. The village district was established in 1907 to bring electric power and water to the summer community. North of the 101 and 1A junction, development thins into salt marsh, small businesses and bungalows. At the spit’s southern end, most of the land is state park, with little development.
